solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Strut for instance extended across wood (6)

indicators.note: a word stretched out so it reaches across another ends up holding that word inside it

blocks.note: say = for instance, as in 'take, say, London'

explanation.surface: A plank of wood is laid across a gap to serve as a structural strut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strut' looks like a building support in this carpentry scene; it is the verb, to walk showily.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words describe a swaggering, showy walk.

clue.text: Political diplomacy in newspaper, paramilitary offensive originally covered by broadcaster (4,5)

indicators.note: the newspaper is placed in the broadcaster, alongside the next piece
the words are reduced to how they originally begin, their first letters
the broadcaster is laid over the other pieces like a cover, so they end up inside it

blocks.note: a sower broadcasts seed by scattering it

explanation.surface: A news report on a paramilitary attack, seen through a TV broadcaster's coverage.
explanation.walkthrough: The broadcaster is not a TV station but a farmer scattering seed by hand, the older sense of broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: A political term: soft power means winning influence by persuasion and attraction rather than force, which is diplomacy's work.

clue.text: Wobbly thing lets in winter air (6,5)

indicators.note: something wobbly will not hold steady, so its letters shift out of order

explanation.surface: A draughty, rickety window or door is letting the cold winter air in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winter air' reads as a cold draught; an air is also a tune, and this one is a Christmas carol.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the carol is a tune sung at Christmas, and air is the old word for a tune.

clue.text: Solvent, take note, capitalist is bearing up! (7)

indicators.note: the phrase bears, carries, the answer within its letters
in a down clue, a word going up is read from bottom to top, backwards

explanation.surface: A capitalist, financially solvent, tells everyone to take note of how well he is doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solvent' plays as the adjective, able to pay debts, which suits the capitalist; it is the noun, a liquid that dissolves things.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: acetone is a common solvent, the main ingredient of nail-varnish remover.

clue.text: Robust second wine, measure of its strength? (10)

blocks.note: s = second, the unit of time
hock is the British name for German white wine from the Rhine
proof is the scale for alcoholic strength

explanation.surface: A wine buff praises a robust second wine and wonders how strong it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robust' looks like a tasting note on the wine; it is the definition, meaning sturdy.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: something built to withstand knocks without damage is robust.

clue.text: Go jump in a lake, as might frog? (3,2)

blocks.note: a rude way of telling someone to go away
what a frog does to get into the water, taken literally

explanation.surface: Telling someone to get lost, with a frog as the one who would literally jump in.
explanation.walkthrough: HOP IT is British slang for 'go away', and the frog takes the phrase literally, hopping into the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom matched with an idiom: both are brusque British ways of telling someone to leave.

clue.text: Might prove enchanting framing lovers starting out — might it? (11)

definitions.text: Might prove enchanting framing lovers starting out — might it?

indicators.note: a frame goes round a picture, so one word goes round the letter
a word's start is its first letter, so only that is used

explanation.surface: A romantic evening for a couple setting out together, with a hopeful question at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also describes the answer: candlelight round a couple might well prove enchanting, and the closing 'might it?' invites you to see that.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: soft candlelight surrounding a pair of new lovers is the classic enchanting setting.

clue.text: Resolve to appear bold in a concrete jungle (11)

blocks.note: a concrete jungle is a city

explanation.surface: Someone steels themselves to look confident in a tough urban setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolve' reads as a verb, to make up one's mind; it is the noun, determination.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: stubborn persistence in a purpose is resolve.

clue.text: Greenhouse gas has park warden huffy in the end (8)

indicators.note: only what comes at the end of the word, its final letter, is used

explanation.surface: A grumpy park warden complains about greenhouse gases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greenhouse gas' is a set phrase, but it splits: the greenhouse is the definition and the gas is oxygen.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an orangery is a glass building for growing orange trees, a particular kind of greenhouse.

clue.text: Day and date to eat chicken, primarily, as — this dish has it! (9)

definitions.text: Day and date to eat chicken, primarily, as — this dish has it!

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater, so the outer words take the others in
the primary, first, letter of the word is taken

blocks.note: to see someone = to date them

explanation.surface: A plan for a Friday date over a chicken dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The last words turn the clue on itself: the dish described, chicken eaten on a date, is exactly what a fricassee has in it.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a fricassee is a stew of meat pieces in white sauce, very often chicken.

clue.text: Suggested delicacy one has filled (5)

indicators.note: the letter fills a word the way food fills a stomach, sitting inside it

blocks.note: tact = delicacy in dealing with people

explanation.surface: A food critic reports that a recommended delicacy is one that has filled them up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delicacy' tempts as a treat to eat, and 'filled' backs that up; here it means tact.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: what is tacit is implied without being said outright, so merely suggested.

clue.text: Roman emperor’s bronze embodying power (6)

indicators.note: to embody something is to take it into your body, so the word holds the other inside

blocks.note: a tan is a bronzed skin colour
the Raj = British rule in India

explanation.surface: A bronze statue of a Roman emperor that embodies imperial power.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a museum label, and bronze belongs there as a metal; it is the colour of a suntan.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Trajan ruled Rome from AD 98 to 117.

clue.text: Cherry? Round object sustaining insect (7,4)

indicators.note: to sustain is to hold up, and in a down clue the lower part holds up the upper

blocks.note: a cricket is a chirping insect

explanation.surface: A cherry described as a small round thing, with a bug on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket is the bat-and-ball game played across Britain and the Commonwealth, and its commentators call the shiny new red ball the cherry.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang use from cricket: the new ball is the cherry, from its red colour.

clue.text: Projection: all but one in football team active (5)

blocks.clueFragment: all but one in football team
blocks.note: a football team has eleven players

explanation.surface: A prediction that ten of a football side's eleven will be in action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Projection' suggests a forecast in this sporting surface; it is a piece sticking out.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodworking term: the tenon is the tongue that projects from one timber to fit a mortise in another.

clue.text: Laughing stock, ordinary bloke on feet to welcome king (8,4)

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to let them in, so the bloke takes the king inside

explanation.surface: An ordinary man gets to his feet to greet the king and is laughed at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock' in the definition has nothing to do with farming or finance; a laughing stock is a person everyone mocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Two idioms for the same thing: a person or thing that is constantly and predictably mocked.

clue.text: Cigarette lit, fire heartlessly put out (6,3)

indicators.note: a word without its heart has lost its middle, leaving only the outside letters
letters that are out of place are no longer in their proper order

blocks.note: put with its middle U gone

explanation.surface: A cigarette has been lit and the fire then put out carelessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like one phrase for extinguishing; it splits, with put losing its heart and out the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a filter tip is a cigarette with a filter at the mouth end.

clue.text: Concept about country in South Africa regulating process (13)

indicators.note: about means around, so the concept goes round everything else
the country is placed in South Africa, inside its abbreviation

blocks.note: Mali is a West African country

explanation.surface: A political idea concerning one African state inside another.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: the country first goes into RSA, and that whole group then goes into the concept.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: normalisation is the process of bringing things into line with a norm, which regulates them.

clue.text: Lighter game (7)

blocks.note: a lighter is a flat-bottomed barge
a card game, the British name for blackjack

explanation.surface: A less serious game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lighter' reads as an adjective; it is the noun, a flat barge that carries cargo to and from ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a pontoon is a flat-bottomed boat like a lighter, and pontoon is also the card game known elsewhere as blackjack.

clue.text: Effective narration (7)

blocks.note: as a blow or argument that hits home
as in the act of recounting a story

explanation.surface: Praise for a gripping piece of storytelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words sit side by side like a review's verdict, but each is a separate definition: one adjective, one noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: as an adjective it means striking and effective, as a noun the act of recounting a story.

clue.text: Pose adopted by boy in a state? (7)

definitions.note: ALASKAN names a person; 'in a state' describes where they are

indicators.note: an adopted child is taken into a family, so the word is taken inside the boy's name

blocks.note: to pose a question = to ask it

explanation.surface: A child in care strikes an attitude, clearly worked up about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a state' suggests being upset; it is one of the US states.
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading of an idiom: someone from Alaska lives in a US state, so is quite literally in a state.

clue.text: Huge flier off course, rare bird on course? (9,9)

blocks.note: in golf, an albatross is three under par on a hole

explanation.surface: A huge bird has strayed from its route, a rarity turning up on a golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'course's differ: a route, then a golf course, where birdie, eagle and albatross are ever-rarer scores below par.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: this seabird has the largest wingspan of any living bird.

clue.text: Word of sympathy received by prophet, understood (8)

indicators.note: what is received is taken in, so the prophet takes the word inside him

blocks.note: Gad is a prophet in the Old Testament
'there, there' is said to comfort someone

explanation.surface: A prophet hears a kind word and takes the point.
explanation.walkthrough: Gad is a minor figure, the prophet who advised King David; the usual crossword prophets are ELI and AMOS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'I gathered' and 'I understood' both mean grasped from what was said.

clue.text: Higher than the first sixteen characters? (4)

blocks.note: from the first letter of the alphabet to the sixteenth

explanation.surface: A question about the opening letters of the alphabet.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as A TO P: from A, the first letter, to P, the sixteenth.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a preposition meaning on top of, and a spelled-out range of the alphabet.

clue.text: Drunk sizing up a pasty? (3-4)

explanation.surface: A drunk eyes up a pasty on the way home from the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads the slang word literally: a pasty, a British pastry with a savoury filling, is a sort of pie, and sizing it up is eyeing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang term, read once as intended and once literally.

clue.text: Meat cut, a doctor and companion tucked in (4,4)

indicators.note: things tucked in are pushed inside, like a shirt into trousers

explanation.surface: A butcher's cut of meat tucked into by a doctor and a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meat cut' looks like the definition in one piece, especially with the answer a cut; only 'Meat' defines, and the cut belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a lamb chop is one kind of meat.

clue.text: Principled observance declared? (5)

indicators.note: what is declared is said out loud, so the word counts only by its sound

blocks.note: a rite is a religious observance

explanation.surface: A question about whether a publicly declared ritual is a matter of principle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principled' is an adjective, so the answer is right in its moral sense, not a noun like an entitlement.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a right action is morally correct, as a principled one is.

clue.text: Peg, callous sister upset youngster (8)

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so in a down clue the word is turned bottom to top

blocks.note: a golf tee is a peg for the ball
Regan, King Lear's cruel daughter, sister of Goneril and Cordelia, reversed

explanation.surface: Peg is upset by her unfeeling sister, a sulky youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peg' poses as a girl's name at the start; it is a golf tee. The callous sister is Shakespeare's Regan.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a teenager, aged thirteen to nineteen, is one kind of youngster.

clue.text: Take it in your own hands and chill out! (3,1,4)

definitions.text: Take it in your own hands

blocks.clueFragment: Take it in your own hands
blocks.note: to take hold of something physically
an order to calm down and pull yourself together

explanation.surface: Advice to someone in a flap: take control yourself and calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take it in your own hands' sounds like taking charge; read literally, it is grasping something.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: literally, to grasp something; as an idiom, a command to stop panicking.

clue.text: Have the temerity to bring in European regulation where Dover is (8)

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside, so the outer word takes the others

blocks.note: to dare = to have the nerve

explanation.surface: A cross-Channel row about daring to impose EU rules at the port of Dover.
explanation.walkthrough: Dover wants to be the English Channel port, which fits the European rules; it is also the capital of the US state of Delaware.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by fact: Dover is Delaware's state capital.

clue.text: Quiet moment in corporation, activists quickly dispersing (5,3)

indicators.note: the first pieces are put in the last one, inside it

blocks.note: corporation is jokey old slang for a paunch
mo = moment, as in 'half a mo'

explanation.surface: A pause at a company as protesters break up and leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' plays as a company but is old slang for a pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a flash mob gathers suddenly in public to perform, then melts away fast.

clue.text: A border sign breaking three times now (2,3,6)

indicators.note: the pieces break into another group, splitting it apart

blocks.note: a hem is a border of cloth

explanation.surface: A sign on a border crossing is broken three times.
explanation.walkthrough: The break comes late, between the second and third T, which is why the letters are hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the phrase means at the present time, now.

clue.text: Missing intro, musical group provides backing (7)

indicators.note: a song missing its intro has lost its opening, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a band's bass players, as a group

explanation.surface: A band without its opening number still supplies the backing music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' fits the musical surface as a backing band; it means support.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: to assist is to back someone up with help.

clue.text: Stomach after lemon chicken (11)

indicators.note: the stomach comes after, following the lemon in the answer

blocks.note: lemon is a shade of yellow

explanation.surface: A recipe: lemon chicken, something to stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lemon chicken' looks like one dish; lemon is wordplay and chicken, a coward, is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang synonym: both words are informal for a coward.

clue.text: Spillage of tear, or novice crying over spilt milk? (12)

indicators.note: spilt things scatter and land any which way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A beginner weeps over a spilled drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the proverb 'it's no use crying over spilt milk', about fussing over something trivial and past.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: crying over spilt milk is getting upset out of proportion to a small loss.

clue.text: Smashing up of gate amuses a pig, perhaps (7,4)

indicators.note: something smashed up is in pieces, so the letters are broken and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A pig finds it funny to smash through a farm gate.
explanation.walkthrough: The pig is not the animal in the farmyard picture but what it ends up as.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example turned round: sausagemeat is minced pork, and a pig is one source of it.

clue.text: Looking at wall, where ladder goes in a difficult position? (2,7,2)

definitions.text: Looking at wall, where ladder goes

blocks.clueFragment: Looking at wall, where ladder goes
blocks.note: a ladder leans upright on a wall, facing it
the idiom for being in trouble

explanation.surface: Someone facing a wall, with a ladder leaning on it, is in an awkward spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is read literally first, a ladder propped on the wall, then as the idiom for being in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: literally, leaning on a wall; as an idiom, facing serious difficulties.

clue.text: Mean and ready for bare-knuckle fight? (5-6)

explanation.surface: A nasty character spoiling for a fistfight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' reads as nasty alongside the fight; it means stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the idiom for stingy, and a literal clenching of the fists.

clue.text: Certain kennels benefit hot dog! (6,5)

indicators.note: to kennel a dog is to house it, so the outer word houses the others

explanation.surface: A kennels' fundraising event selling hot dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kennels' plays as the dogs' home; it is the verb, to house. 'Hot dog' is a snack in the surface but splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the basset hound is a short-legged, long-eared breed of dog.

clue.text: Having experienced a close shave, tie felt different going in front (11)

indicators.note: the letters are made different by being put in another order
the rearranged letters go into another word

blocks.note: a very close shave leaves you bald

explanation.surface: A man who narrowly escaped disaster now feels differently about going to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A close shave' is a near miss in the surface but is taken literally, as a razor to the scalp.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: in war the front is where the fighting is, the battlefield.

clue.text: Nub: link with heat that’s off, not on (11)

indicators.note: letters that are off are out of their place, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cooker has a heating element that's switched off, not on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off, not on' sounds like a switch; 'not on' is British for unacceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom: something 'not on' is out of the question, too unacceptable to consider.

clue.text: Box opened by one with black key (5,3)

indicators.note: the word is opened up so others can go inside it

blocks.note: an ace counts one in cards

explanation.surface: A box is unlocked with a black key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' and 'key' look like a locked box; box is the verb, to fight, and the key is on a keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the space bar is the long key at the bottom of a keyboard.

clue.text: Where nation goes for oath on page, poisonous stuff (9)

blocks.note: N (nation) is placed after DAM to spell DAMN, an oath

explanation.surface: A newspaper page on where the country is heading, and the toxic content printed there.
explanation.walkthrough: An unusual device: the clue asks where N goes to make an oath, and the answer to that question supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mining term: afterdamp is the poisonous gas, mostly carbon monoxide, left after an explosion underground.

clue.text: Perhaps ticker in particular good before brief turns (3,5)

indicators.note: a word that turns round faces the other way, so it reads backwards

explanation.surface: A heart, perhaps, in good shape before short bouts of exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ticker' is slang for the heart; here it is something that ticks, and 'perhaps' marks the answer as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a kitchen egg timer may tick away the minutes.

clue.text: Deck held in casino, it appearing to the left (5)

indicators.note: the answer is held inside the words that follow
in an across clue, text running to the left runs backwards

blocks.note: casinO IT APpearing, read right to left

explanation.surface: A deck of cards is held at a casino table and shown to the player on the left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' is a pack of cards in the casino picture; it is an outdoor platform.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a patio and a deck are both outdoor areas beside a house for sitting out.

clue.text: Getting better marks coming in last? (2,3,4)

indicators.note: the letter comes in, entering the phrase

blocks.note: last in line = on the end
M = marks, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A student's grades are improving though they still come in last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' suggests school grades in the surface; it is the old German currency.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone on the mend is recovering from illness or injury.

clue.text: Pulp eaten by bird, sticky thing (8)

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside the eater, so the bird takes the pulp in

blocks.note: a flyer = a bird, something that flies

explanation.surface: A bird eats mushy food and ends up with something stuck to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is not a species but anything that flies, a flyer.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: flypaper is coated with glue to trap flies.

clue.text: Playwright confident in speech? (4)

indicators.note: in speech a word is heard, not seen, so only its sound matters

explanation.surface: A playwright who sounds very sure of himself when he talks.
explanation.walkthrough: The homophone needs a southern British accent, where the R in sure is silent and it rhymes with law.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: George Bernard Shaw was the Irish playwright who wrote Pygmalion.

clue.text: Macbeth’s life identity: a ballad too stupid? (1,4,4,2,2,5)

annotation.answer: A TALE TOLD BY AN IDIOT

indicators.note: stupid letters have lost their sense, so they are jumbled up

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a ballad about Macbeth's identity is too foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Macbeth, life 'is a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing'. The indicator 'stupid' echoes the idiot of the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: A quotation: Macbeth's 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow' speech describes life in exactly these words.

clue.text: Cooler leader in actuality behind a web of deceit? (4,3)

indicators.note: threads in a web are tangled together, so the letters are tangled
the leader of a word is its first letter
the letter goes behind, after the rest

explanation.surface: A cool leader who is in fact hiding behind a tangle of lies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' looks like a comparative adjective about the leader; it is a noun, a cold drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a cooler is a cold drink, and iced tea is a classic one.

clue.text: Spirited opening of performance, promising (6)

indicators.note: as a show's opening is its very start, the word's first letter is used

explanation.surface: A theatre review of a lively, promising first night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' reads as an opening night; it points to the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean brave and full of spirit.

clue.text: Incompetent type, one blowing something out of proportion, ultimately (7)

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so only the word's last letter is used

blocks.note: last letter of proportion, which the bugler blows into his instrument

explanation.surface: A clumsy person who blows things out of proportion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blowing something out of proportion' is an idiom for exaggerating; here it splits into a bugler and a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a bungler does things clumsily, an incompetent sort.

clue.text: Suit: fine one, choice clothes (5)

indicators.note: as clothes go round a body, the word wraps round the others

blocks.note: your best bet = your best choice

explanation.surface: A tailor's note: a good suit, one fine choice of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' and 'clothes' are tailoring in the surface; suit is the verb, and clothes is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, in the verb sense: what befits you is appropriate to you.

clue.text: Tender secretary at length scrubbing back (7)

indicators.note: the back of the word is scrubbed out, removing its last letter

blocks.note: in full = at length, losing its last L

explanation.surface: A secretary spends ages scrubbing someone's back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' sounds loving in this bath-time picture; it means sore.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a tender spot hurts when touched.

clue.text: Part of jacket, copy reading between the lines? (5)

indicators.note: the copy is read between the two lines, sitting with one on each side

explanation.surface: A book jacket's blurb, and a copy of it read for hidden meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reading between the lines' is the idiom for spotting hidden meaning; here it places the copy inside two Ls.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by part: the lapel is the folded-back front edge of a jacket's collar.

clue.text: Eg plane orbiting Klingon kingdom identified initially — by one of those? (7)

indicators.note: a body in orbit circles round another, so the tree goes round the letters
each word gives only its initial, the letter it starts with

blocks.note: first letters of Klingon Kingdom Identified

explanation.surface: A spaceship circles an alien empire, recognised straight away by a sci-fi fan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plane' plays as an aircraft or spacecraft; it is the tree. The definition points back: a Klingon kingdom is what a Trekkie would spot at once.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by reference: Klingons come from Star Trek, and 'one of those' is a fan of the show.

clue.text: Rendering of a perfect theme in pastoral scene (4,9)

indicators.note: a rendering is a new version, so the letters are rendered in a new order

explanation.surface: An artist's rendering of an ideal subject in a country landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about painting, and fittingly the answer names a genre of painting, as in Watteau's scenes of people at leisure outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowed French term: a fête champêtre is an outdoor country party, and a painting of one is a pastoral scene.

clue.text: A bolt screwed into rod one’s pocketed! (4,5)

indicators.note: a thing screwed is twisted round, so the letters are twisted into a new order
the rearranged letters go into another word

explanation.surface: A bolt is screwed into a rod, and someone has walked off with one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pocketed' suggests stolen; the definition means fitted with pockets.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the table used for pool has six pockets for the balls.

clue.text: Mangy spud, by the sound of it? (5)

indicators.note: judged only by the sound of it, so the spelling may change

blocks.note: tattie is Scottish and Northern English for potato

explanation.surface: A scruffy-looking potato.
explanation.walkthrough: A spud is a potato, and tattie is the Scottish word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: both describe something shabby and worn.

clue.text: Standard trick nailing a rudiment of drumming (10)

blocks.note: to diddle = to cheat, trick; it is nailed on after A

explanation.surface: A standard trick for nailing the basics of drumming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nailing' reads as mastering in the surface; here it only fixes A to the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A drumming term: the paradiddle, sticked RLRR LRLL, is one of the standard rudiments drummers learn.

clue.text: Strong programme cut, smoke remains? (3,3)

indicators.note: the word is cut short, losing its last letter

blocks.note: f = forte, loud or strong in music
an agenda is a programme, minus its last A

explanation.surface: A strong schedule is trimmed back, but the smoking habit remains.
explanation.walkthrough: A fag is British slang for a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A British slang term: the stub left when a cigarette has been smoked.
